study.title: 1 Kings 11 The spiritual fall of Solomon and the beginning of the division of the kingdom
study.overview: The chapter shows the painful contrast between the wisdom received by Solomon and the infidelity that marked his last years. The king, who was to remain utterly loyal to the LORD, multiplied wives, tolerated and promoted idolatry, and thus provoked divine wrath. God's answer is not only to discipline Solomon personally, but to announce the rupture of the kingdom, even though preserving a share of David's sake and because of Jerusalem. The chapter ends with the death of Solomon and the succession of Rehoboam, preparing the stage for the division of Israel.

outline.title: Disordered Love and Idolaria
outline.explanation: Solomon is attached to many foreign women, contrary to the commandment of the LORD. In old age, his heart turns away to other gods; he proceeds to do evil, builds high for pagan deities, and legitimizes the idolatrous cult to please his women.

outline.title: The wrath of the LORD and the sentence on the kingdom
outline.explanation: God is angry because Solomon, despite having received direct revelations, did not keep the covenant or the statutes. The divine sentence announces the division of the kingdom, but postpones the complete judgment for love of David and preserves a tribe for Solomon's son.

outline.title: Adversaries raised against Solomon
outline.explanation: The LORD raises up external enemies: Hadad, the Edomite, and Rezom, who trouble Israel during all the reign of Solomon. The text shows that political disorder is also an expression of God's judgment on the king's disobedience.

outline.title: Jeroboam, the promise of division, and the end of the reign
outline.explanation: Jeroboam appears as a new adversary and the prophet Ahijah announces, through the gesture of the torn garment, that ten tribes will be given to him. Still, God promises to preserve a tribe because of David and Jerusalem. The chapter concludes with Solomon's attempt to kill Jeroboam, his flight to Egypt, the final assessment of the reign, and the king's death.

study.context: The text does not depend on many external data to be understood: it relies on the memory of the covenant of the LORD with Israel, in the choice of Jerusalem as a special place and in the figure of David as a reference of fidelity. The notes indicate that the division of the kingdom begins here and that the conclusion mentions another historical record that is lost today, used as a source for the narrative of the Kings.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that spiritual gifts, wisdom, and elevated position do not nullify the responsibility of obedience. Solomon's idolatry is not treated as a private fault, but as a sin with public and national consequences. God remains holy in judging the king; at the same time, he remains faithful to his promises to David, showing that his discipline does not degate his covenant. The preservation of a tribe and the promise to Jeroboam reveal that the Lord rules the political history of Israel, using even adversaries and ruptures to fulfill his purposes. The contrast between David, who repented when confronted, and Solomon, who did not persevere in obedience, is also evident.

scholarViews.insight: Solomon's marriage covenants compromised his spiritual fidelity and brought disastrous spiritual and political consequences for the people.
The commentator points out that the chapter begins with a very sad "mas" s, marking Solomon's decay in his last days and his opening to idolatry through foreign women.
The note notes that Solomon had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and uses this to emphasize the extreme dimension of his error and his polygamous house.

questions: What compromises, relationships or habits today can be diverting the heart from faithfulness to the LORD, as happened to Solomon?
How does God's discipline in this chapter show at the same time his holiness and his faithfulness to the promises made to David?
How can a person's spiritual and moral leadership affect the destiny of a whole community?
study.practice: Examine honestly what allegiance they compete with obedience to God in your life. Pray for a whole heart, without division, and take concrete measures to cut off influences that push you away from the Lord. At the same time, remember that God is faithful to his promises: when there is repentance, hope is not lost, but needs to walk along with real obedience. If you occupies an influence position, consider that private choices can produce lasting public effects.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow you to safely determine many details about the exact chronology of opponents or the historical extension of the sources mentioned at the end of the chapter. It is also not possible to affirm, only from this material, which women of Solomon would have changed from religion or as each cultual construction was administered in every detail. The reference to "a tribe" and relations with Jerusalem is presented in the text itself as part of the divine sentence, but the chapter itself does not develop all later developments.
